title: Protocols
overview: Protocols are agreed rules that let unlike hardware and software communicate reliably. At A2 the central model is the four-layer TCP/IP stack, plus the purposes of common application protocols such as HTTP, FTP, POP3, IMAP, SMTP and BitTorrent.
syllabusPoints: Explain why protocols and layered protocol stacks are used.
Describe the Application, Transport, Internet and Link layers of TCP/IP.
Explain how data is encapsulated on transmission and decapsulated on receipt.
State the purposes of HTTP, FTP, POP3, IMAP, SMTP and BitTorrent.

definitions.definition: An agreed set of rules for formatting, transmitting, receiving and interpreting data.
A layered collection of protocols, each layer providing a defined service.
Adding headers/control information as data passes down the stack.
A number used by the transport layer to identify an application/service on a host.
The internet protocol suite organised into Application, Transport, Internet and Link layers.

sections.title: Why layers are useful
content: Layering separates responsibilities. An application can use transport services without knowing network hardware details; local-network technology can change without redesigning every application. Standard interfaces improve interoperability, maintenance and troubleshooting.

sections.title: Application layer
content: Provides network services directly used by software. HTTP/HTTPS transfer web content, FTP transfers files, SMTP sends email, POP3/IMAP retrieve or manage email, and BitTorrent supports peer-to-peer distribution.

sections.title: Transport layer
content: Provides end-to-end application communication. TCP can segment data, number segments, detect loss, request retransmission and reassemble data. Port numbers identify the target application/service.

sections.title: Internet layer
content: Uses logical IP addressing and routing. Routers examine destination information and forward packets towards the destination network.

sections.title: Link layer
content: Handles frames and transmission across the local medium, including local hardware addressing and access to technologies such as Ethernet or Wi-Fi.

sections.title: Encapsulation in practice
content: At the sender, application data moves down the stack and receives layer-specific control information; the receiver removes that information in reverse order and passes the reconstructed data up to the application.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.content:
Sender: Application -> Transport -> Internet -> Link
Receiver: Link -> Internet -> Transport -> Application

examTips: Use precise protocol verbs: SMTP sends; POP3/IMAP retrieve/manage; FTP transfers files.
Keep IP addresses and port numbers distinct.
If asked why a stack helps, mention modularity/standardisation/interoperability.
commonMistakes: Putting routing in the Application layer.
Calling TCP/IP just two protocols rather than a protocol suite.
